root.name: Ruy Lopez: Bird's Defense Deferred
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nd4

parent.name: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6
parent.overview: 3...a6 is the main road of the Ruy Lopez (roughly two thirds to 90 per cent of Ruy games per the sources). It asks White's bishop an immediate question: Bxc6 (Exchange) or the retreat 4.Ba4, after which Black can play ...b5 to kick the bishop again. The main line is the Closed Ruy (5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3), a locked, slow centre where White builds the c3-d4 pawn duo and reroutes the knight Nb1-d2-f1-g3, and Black seeks queenside counterplay with ...c5/...c4 or ...Bb7 and ...Re8/...Bf8. Alternatives at move five or later include the Open Variation (5...Nxe4), the Arkhangelsk (5...b5), and Marshall Attack (8...d5), with Anti-Marshall systems used by White to dodge it. Play is typically slow positional manoeuvring (the 'Spanish torture': a small White edge pressed for forty moves) with very deep theory. It has been a main weapon of nearly every world champion.

root.name: Scandinavian Defense: Kádas Gambit
root.moves: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Nf6 3. d4 c6 4. dxc6 e5

parent.name: Scandinavian Defense: Modern Variation
parent.overview: Black answers 2.exd5 by developing the knight and delaying the recapture, avoiding the tempo lost when the queen takes on d5. The main line is 3.d4 Nxd5 (the Marshall, as the old name had it), after which 4.Nf3 and 4.c4 Nb6 or ...Bg4 give White a space edge and Black quick development and easy piece play. White can also hold the pawn with 3.c4 (Black strikes back with ...c6 into Panov-type structures, or the Icelandic Gambit 3...e6) or play 3.Bb5+ Bd7. Wikipedia/Emms describe the 2...Nf6 lines as the more tactical branch of the Scandinavian, though sound for Black; White usually keeps a slight initiative through development. Positions are usually open or semi-open with Caro-Kann-like pawn formations (...c6, ...e6) and Black often castles short while White controls more space.

parent.name: Polish Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.b4 to grab queenside space and fianchetto the bishop to b2, putting long-diagonal pressure on e5, f6 and g7. It is an irregular flank opening: Black chooses the set-up with 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Bxb4 3.Bxe5, the Exchange Variation, which equalises), 1...d5 (the German Defence 2...Qd6 etc.), or 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 reaching Indian-like or Queen's Gambit-like set-ups. The opening is sound and not refuted but gives Black no real problems, so it is rarely seen at elite level and chosen as a surprise weapon (Carlsen used it against Nakamura and So in 2021). Theory is small and the play is flank-oriented, with unbalanced pawn structures but typically no early forced tactics. Alekhine's complaint was that it reveals White's intentions before knowing Black's.

root.name: London System: Poisoned Pawn Variation
root.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. Nf3 d5 3. Bf4 c5 4. e3 Qb6 5. Nc3

parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: London System
parent.overview: The London is a set-up rather than a line: White builds d4, e3, c3 with Bf4, Nf3, Nbd2, Bd3 and castles, adjusting the details but not the plan, against almost anything Black plays. The usual aim is a knight on e5 backed by pawns and the bishop, then either a kingside attack (Bxh7+ ideas, Rf3-h3, a queen to the b1-h7 diagonal) or a central break with e4 or c4. Black's main counterplay is ...c5 and ...Qb6 against b2, plus ...Bf5, ...Nh5 or ...Bd6 to challenge the f4 bishop, or a kingside fianchetto. Move order matters: the root here (2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bf4) is only one way in; the same set-up arises from 2.Bf4 first (Accelerated London, D00), from 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 followed by Bf4, and against Indian set-ups, so a page for this root describes the system as a whole. Sources agree it is solid with low theory and closed or semi-closed play, and that it is criticised as repetitive and short on dynamism at the top, though Carlsen, Kamsky, Aronian, Radjabov and Ding Liren have all used it.
